formulas.tex: D^{k}_x(y) = \text{least cost of an } x\text{–}y \text{ path with at most } k \text{ links}, \qquad \text{rounds} = h \le N - 1
formulas.text: D^k_x(y) = least cost of an x–y path with at most k links; rounds to converge = h ≤ N − 1
where: rounds counted from tables that hold only the router itself
largest number of links on any least-cost path
formulas.note: Tables that already hold the direct link costs are the state k = 1, so after e exchanges the estimates cover paths of at most e + 1 links.

formulas.name: Dijkstra relaxation in link state routing
where: the router just made permanent, the one with the smallest tentative distance
formulas.note: Repeat until every router is permanent. The next hop to a destination is the first router on its shortest path. O(N²) with an array, O(E log N) with a heap.

problemTypes.title: Network, broadcast, host range and host count from IP/n
recipe: Write the mask and find the octet where it is neither 255 nor 0; the block size there is 256 minus that mask octet.
Network: round that octet of the address down to a multiple of the block size and set every later octet to 0.
Broadcast: network octet + block size − 1 in that octet, and 255 in every later octet.
Hosts run from network + 1 to broadcast − 1, and there are 2^(32 − n) − 2 of them.
problemTypes.trap: Treating the block as a /24 and changing only the last octet when the prefix ends in the third octet.

problemTypes.title: Dividing or allocating a block: subnets, VLSM and valid allocations
recipe: Equal subnets: borrow s bits for 2ˢ subnets, each with 2^(32 − n − s) − 2 hosts.
Required sizes: choose each prefix from its host count, and allocate the largest block first.
Check every block in every option: it must start on a multiple of its own size, lie inside the parent block and overlap no other block.
problemTypes.trap: Accepting an allocation whose start is not aligned, such as a /21 that starts at third octet 36.

problemTypes.title: Forwarding by longest prefix match
recipe: For each table entry, check whether the destination's first n bits equal the prefix, i.e. whether it lies between the entry's network and broadcast addresses.
Among the matching entries, take the one with the largest n.
Use the default route 0.0.0.0/0 only if no other entry matches.
problemTypes.trap: Taking the first matching row of the table instead of the longest match.

problemTypes.title: Aggregating contiguous blocks into one prefix
recipe: Write the varying octet of the first and last block in binary and count the leading bits common to the whole range.
Check that the blocks are consecutive, that there are 2ᵏ of the same size, and that the first starts on a multiple of the combined size.
The aggregate is /(n − k) for 2ᵏ blocks of /n.
problemTypes.trap: Aggregating blocks that are not aligned, which would also claim addresses that belong to someone else.

problemTypes.title: Fragment count, offsets, MF flags and lengths
recipe: Find the data to carry: the original Total Length minus its header.
Data per fragment: MTU minus the fragment header, rounded down to a multiple of 8.
Fragments = ⌈data / per-fragment data⌉; offsets run 0, d/8, 2d/8, …; MF = 1 on all but the last.
The last fragment carries the remainder; each fragment's Total Length is its data plus its header.
If a fragment is split again, repeat with the new MTU, add its own offset to each piece's offset, and give the last piece the fragment's MF flag.
problemTypes.trap: Forgetting to round MTU − header down to a multiple of 8, or giving the offset in bytes instead of 8-byte units.

problemTypes.title: Distance vector table update
recipe: For each destination, add the cost of the link to each neighbour to that neighbour's advertised distance.
Take the minimum; the neighbour that achieves it is the next hop.
Ignore the router's own old entries unless the question says otherwise; its distance to itself stays 0.
For 'after e exchanges' questions starting from direct link costs, the estimate is the least cost over paths of at most e + 1 links.
problemTypes.trap: Picking the neighbour with the smallest advertised distance, or the cheapest link, instead of the smallest sum.

problemTypes.title: Forwarding table from link state information
recipe: Run Dijkstra from the router: repeatedly make permanent the router with the smallest tentative distance and relax its links.
Record each destination's predecessor, then trace back to find the first hop out of the source.
The table holds the cost and the first hop for every destination.
problemTypes.trap: Choosing the path with the fewest hops, or the direct link, when a longer path is cheaper.

problemTypes.title: Count to infinity after a link failure
recipe: Note which routes used the failed link and what each neighbour is still advertising.
Recompute with Bellman-Ford using those stale vectors: a router may adopt a route that leads back through itself.
Repeat exchange by exchange; with split horizon or poison reverse, drop the advertisement back to the neighbour the route was learned from.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming the router marks the destination unreachable at once; without split horizon it accepts the stale route.

questions.stem: A host has the address 172.16.45.200/21. What is the broadcast address of its network?
questions.explanation: /21 leaves 11 host bits and the mask is 255.255.248.0, so the third octet moves in blocks of 256 − 248 = 8. 45 lies in the block 40–47, so the network is 172.16.40.0 and the broadcast address, with every host bit 1, is 172.16.47.255. Usable hosts run from 172.16.40.1 to 172.16.47.254, 2046 in all. 172.16.45.255 treats the block as a /24, 172.16.40.255 sets only the last octet's host bits, and 172.16.63.255 is the answer for /19.

questions.stem: How many host addresses can be assigned in an IPv4 block with prefix length /22, given that its network and broadcast addresses cannot be assigned?
questions.explanation: A /22 leaves 32 − 22 = 10 host bits, so the block holds 2¹⁰ = 1024 addresses. Removing the network address (host bits all 0) and the broadcast address (host bits all 1) leaves 1022.

questions.stem: The block 192.168.1.0/24 is divided into equal /27 subnets. How many subnets are there, and how many usable host addresses does each have?
options: 8 subnets, 32 hosts each
8 subnets, 30 hosts each
6 subnets, 30 hosts each
16 subnets, 14 hosts each
questions.explanation: Going from /24 to /27 borrows 3 bits, giving 2³ = 8 subnets. Each keeps 5 host bits: 2⁵ = 32 addresses, of which 30 are usable once the network and broadcast addresses are removed. 32 forgets those two, 6 applies the obsolete rule that discards the all-0s and all-1s subnets, and 16 subnets of 14 hosts is the split into /28.

questions.stem: An ISP holds 130.40.32.0/20. It gives half of these addresses to organisation X and a quarter to organisation Y, and keeps the rest. Which allocation is valid?
questions.explanation: The /20 spans third octets 32–47. Half of it is a /21 (8 values of the third octet) and a quarter is a /22 (4 values), and each block must start on a multiple of its own size. X = 130.40.32.0/21 with Y = 130.40.40.0/22 gives X 32–39 and Y 40–43, leaving 44–47 to the ISP. 130.40.36.0/21 is not a valid block: a /21 must start at a multiple of 8, and the /21 holding 36 is 32–39, which overlaps Y's 32–35. Y = 130.40.36.0/22 covers 36–39, inside X's 32–39. A /22 and a /23 hand out a quarter and an eighth, not a half and a quarter.

questions.stem: A router's forwarding table has these entries: 10.0.0.0/8 → eth0, 10.16.0.0/12 → eth1, 10.20.0.0/16 → eth2, 10.20.128.0/17 → eth3, and the default route 0.0.0.0/0 → eth4. On which interfaces does it forward datagrams for 10.20.200.1, 10.40.1.1 and 10.25.1.1, in that order?
options: eth3, eth0, eth1
eth2, eth0, eth1
eth3, eth1, eth1
eth3, eth0, eth0
questions.explanation: 10.20.200.1 matches the /8, the /12, the /16 and the /17, which covers 10.20.128.0–10.20.255.255; the longest is the /17, so eth3. 10.40.1.1 matches only 10.0.0.0/8, because 10.16.0.0/12 spans second octets 16–31: eth0. 10.25.1.1 matches the /8 and the /12 but not 10.20.0.0/16, so the /12 wins: eth1. The default route is used only when nothing else matches.

questions.stem: An ISP owns the four blocks 160.12.64.0/22, 160.12.68.0/22, 160.12.72.0/22 and 160.12.76.0/22 and wants to advertise them as one CIDR prefix that covers exactly these addresses. What is the prefix length of that advertisement?
questions.explanation: The third octets run from 64 to 79: 16 consecutive values starting at 64 = 01000000, a multiple of 16. All of them share the first 4 bits, 0100, of the third octet, so 8 + 8 + 4 = 20 bits are common. The aggregate 160.12.64.0/20 holds exactly the 4 × 1024 = 4096 addresses of the four /22 blocks.

questions.stem: What is the Identification field of the IPv4 header used for?
options: Detecting corruption of the header in transit
Naming the transport protocol carried in the payload
Letting the destination tell which fragments belong to the same original datagram
Putting the segments of a TCP connection back in order
questions.explanation: The sending host gives each datagram an identification value and every fragment carries a copy, so the destination can group fragments before reassembling them with the offsets and the MF flag. Header corruption is caught by the header checksum, the payload's protocol is named by the Protocol field (6 for TCP, 17 for UDP), and TCP orders its bytes with its own sequence numbers.

questions.stem: An IPv4 datagram arrives with header length field IHL = 8 and Total Length = 1000. How many bytes of payload does it carry?
questions.explanation: IHL counts 32-bit words, so the header is 8 × 4 = 32 bytes: the 20 fixed bytes plus 12 bytes of options. Total Length counts the whole datagram in bytes, header included, so the payload is 1000 − 32 = 968 bytes. Reading IHL as bytes would give 992.

questions.stem: A router must forward a 3020-byte IPv4 datagram (a 20-byte header with no options and 3000 bytes of data) onto a link whose MTU is 600 bytes. Each fragment carries a 20-byte header. What value does the fragment-offset field hold in the last fragment?
questions.explanation: Each fragment has room for 600 − 20 = 580 data bytes, but every fragment except the last must carry a multiple of 8, so each carries 576. Five such fragments carry 2880 bytes and the sixth, the last, carries the remaining 120. Its first data byte is byte 2880, so its offset is 2880 / 8 = 360; the offsets run 0, 72, 144, 216, 288 and 360. Using 580 bytes per fragment would start the last fragment at byte 2900, which is not even a multiple of 8.

questions.stem: A router receives an IPv4 fragment with IHL = 5, Total Length = 1020, fragment offset = 100 and MF = 1. Data bytes of the original datagram are numbered from 0. Which of the following statements are true?
options: It is the last fragment of the original datagram.
It carries data bytes 800 to 1799 of the original datagram.
The router may reassemble it with the other fragments before forwarding the datagram.
The data that follows it in the original datagram begins at fragment offset 225.
questions.explanation: The header is 5 × 4 = 20 bytes, so the fragment carries 1000 data bytes. Offset 100 puts its first data byte at 100 × 8 = 800, so it holds bytes 800–1799, and the next data starts at byte 1800, offset 225. MF = 1 says more fragments follow, so it is not the last. Only the final destination reassembles; routers forward fragments independently and may even fragment them again.

questions.stem: A 4020-byte IPv4 datagram (20-byte header, 4000 data bytes) crosses a link with MTU 1500 and is split into fragments of 1480, 1480 and 1040 data bytes. The second fragment then reaches a link with MTU 620 and is fragmented again; every header is 20 bytes. Which of the following statements about the pieces of the second fragment are true?
options: The second fragment is split into 3 pieces.
The last of these pieces has MF = 0.
The pieces have fragment offsets 185, 260 and 335.
The last of these pieces has Total Length 280.
questions.explanation: The second fragment carries original bytes 1480–2959 at offset 1480/8 = 185 with MF = 1. On the 620-byte link each piece holds 8 × ⌊600/8⌋ = 600 data bytes, so the 1480 bytes split into 600, 600 and 280: 3 pieces. Offsets count from the original datagram: 185, 185 + 600/8 = 260 and 260 + 75 = 335. The third original fragment still follows, so the last piece keeps MF = 1. Its Total Length is 280 + 20 = 300; 280 is only its data.

questions.stem: Host H (192.168.1.10) sits behind a NAT router whose public address is 203.0.113.5. H opens a TCP connection from port 5000 to a web server at 198.51.100.7, port 80, and the router maps the connection to public port 40001. How does the server's reply arrive at the router, and what does the router do with it?
options: It arrives from 198.51.100.7:80 addressed to 192.168.1.10:5000, and the router forwards it unchanged.
It arrives from 198.51.100.7:80 addressed to 203.0.113.5:40001, and the router rewrites the source to 203.0.113.5:80.
It arrives from 203.0.113.5:40001 addressed to 198.51.100.7:80, and the router rewrites the source to 192.168.1.10:5000.
It arrives from 198.51.100.7:80 addressed to 203.0.113.5:40001, and the router rewrites the destination to 192.168.1.10:5000.
questions.explanation: On the way out the router replaced the source 192.168.1.10:5000 with 203.0.113.5:40001, so the server only ever sees the public address and replies to 203.0.113.5:40001. The router looks up port 40001 in its translation table, rewrites the destination back to 192.168.1.10:5000 and recomputes the checksums. A private address never appears on the public side, and the server's own address and port are left alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about network address translation (NAT) with port translation are true?
options: Many inside hosts can share one public IPv4 address, because each (private address, port) pair is mapped to a different public port.
Packets with source addresses in 172.16.0.0/12 are routed across the public Internet without translation.
An outside host cannot open a connection to an inside host unless a mapping, such as a configured port forward, already exists.
Because it rewrites addresses and ports, the router must recompute the IP header checksum and the TCP or UDP checksum.
questions.explanation: Port translation tells inside hosts apart by the public port each mapping receives, so one public address serves many hosts. The table is filled by outgoing traffic, so an unsolicited inbound connection finds no entry unless one is configured. The TCP and UDP checksums cover a pseudo-header holding the addresses, so they change along with the IP header checksum. 172.16.0.0/12 is an RFC 1918 private range, which public routers do not carry; that is why NAT is needed.

questions.stem: Router R runs distance vector routing. Its links to neighbours P, Q and S cost 4, 2 and 6. It has just received these distance vectors to destinations (A, B, C, D): from P (3, 8, 2, 7), from Q (7, 4, 6, 9) and from S (2, 2, 5, 1). R computes its new table from these vectors alone. What are R's new entries?
options: A: 8 via S, B: 8 via S, C: 6 via P, D: 7 via S
A: 7 via P, B: 6 via Q, C: 6 via P, D: 7 via S
A: 9 via Q, B: 6 via Q, C: 8 via Q, D: 11 via Q
A: 7 via S, B: 6 via Q, C: 6 via P, D: 7 via S
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford adds each link cost to that neighbour's advertisement and keeps the minimum. A: min(4 + 3, 2 + 7, 6 + 2) = 7 via P. B: min(4 + 8, 2 + 4, 6 + 2) = 6 via Q. C: min(4 + 2, 2 + 6, 6 + 5) = 6 via P. D: min(4 + 7, 2 + 9, 6 + 1) = 7 via S. Following the smallest advertised distance puts A and B at 8 via S, and sending everything to the cheapest neighbour Q gives 9, 6, 8 and 11. 'A: 7 via S' pairs the right cost with the wrong next hop, since A via S costs 6 + 2 = 8.

questions.stem: Six routers run distance vector routing over links with these costs: A–B 1, A–C 4, A–D 2, B–C 2, B–E 7, C–D 2, C–E 3, D–F 4 and E–F 1. Each router starts knowing only the costs of its own links. In each exchange every router sends its vector to its neighbours at the same moment and then recomputes with Bellman-Ford. What is A's distance to E after the first exchange?
questions.explanation: The starting tables cover paths of one link, so after one exchange A knows the cheapest paths of at most two links. A has no link to E; the two-link paths are A–B–E = 1 + 7 = 8 and A–C–E = 4 + 3 = 7, so A records 7 via C. The true least cost, 6 over A–B–C–E, needs three links and appears only after the second exchange, and a third exchange changes nothing. Answering 6 ignores the rounds, and 8 follows the cheapest neighbour B.

questions.stem: Routers A, B and C form a line A–B–C with link costs A–B = 2 and B–C = 1, and run distance vector routing without split horizon or poison reverse. In the converged tables B reaches C at distance 1 and A reaches C at distance 3 via B. The link B–C then fails. B notices at once, and before A learns of the failure, B receives A's periodic vector, which still lists C at distance 3. What does B now record as its route to C?
options: Distance 5, via A
Distance 3, via A
Distance 4, via A
Unreachable (infinity)
questions.explanation: With its direct link gone, B's only candidate is A's advertisement: c(B, A) + D_A(C) = 2 + 3 = 5, via A. B cannot tell that A's route to C runs through B itself. A then moves to 2 + 5 = 7 via B, B to 9 via A, and so on, counting up until the metric reaches infinity (16 in RIP) while packets for C bounce between A and B. 3 forgets the link cost and 4 adds the cost of the failed link. With split horizon A would not advertise C to B at all, and with poison reverse it would advertise infinity, so B would mark C unreachable.

questions.stem: Six routers run link state routing over links with these costs: A–B 1, A–C 4, A–D 2, B–C 2, B–E 7, C–D 2, C–E 3, D–F 4 and E–F 1. After running Dijkstra's algorithm, which forwarding-table entries does router A hold for destinations E and F?
options: E: cost 7, next hop C; F: cost 6, next hop D
E: cost 6, next hop B; F: cost 6, next hop D
E: cost 6, next hop B; F: cost 7, next hop B
E: cost 8, next hop B; F: cost 6, next hop D
questions.explanation: From A, Dijkstra fixes B at 1, D at 2, then C at 3 via A–B–C (cheaper than the direct link of cost 4), then E at 6 via A–B–C–E and F at 6 via A–D–F. The next hop is the first router on each path: B for E and D for F. A–C–E costs 7 and A–B–E costs 8, and A–B–C–E–F costs 7, more than A–D–F.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements comparing distance vector and link state routing are true?
options: A link-state advertisement is delivered only to the neighbours of the router that created it.
Count to infinity can occur in distance vector routing but not in link state routing.
A distance vector router sends its vector only to its directly connected neighbours.
After a topology change, link state routing usually converges faster than distance vector routing.
questions.explanation: Distance vector routers trust their neighbours' estimates, so after a failure they can feed each other stale routes and count to infinity; link state routers each compute routes from a complete map, so this cannot happen. Distance vectors go only to neighbours, while link-state advertisements are flooded to every router, which is what gives each router the full topology. Flooding plus local computation is also why link state converges faster.

pitfalls.text: The n in /n counts network bits, and hosts = 2^(32 − n) − 2: the all-0s (network) and all-1s (broadcast) host addresses cannot be assigned.
Fragments are reassembled only at the final destination; routers forward each fragment on its own and may even fragment it again.
TTL counts hops, not seconds: every router decrements it by one and discards the datagram when it reaches 0.
NAT breaks the end-to-end principle: an outside host cannot reach an inside host unless a translation entry already exists.
Every fragment but the last must carry a multiple of 8 data bytes, so round MTU − header down before dividing; offsets are in 8-byte units, not bytes.
IHL counts 4-byte words (IHL = 5 means 20 bytes), while Total Length counts bytes and includes the header.
Longest prefix match picks the most specific matching entry, not the first matching row, and never the default route when a longer prefix matches.
In a distance vector update the next hop is the neighbour with the smallest link cost + advertised distance, not the one with the smallest advertisement or the cheapest link.

errata.claim: Classful addressing: class A has 2^24 hosts per network, class B 2^16 hosts and class C 2^8 hosts.
errata.correction: Those are the numbers of addresses per network. The all-0s and all-1s host addresses are reserved, as the −2 rule for CIDR on the same page says, so the usable hosts are 2²⁴ − 2 = 16 777 214, 2¹⁶ − 2 = 65 534 and 2⁸ − 2 = 254.

errata.claim: IPv6 improvements over IPv4 include 'IPSec mandatory'; the voice note on page 644 repeats 'mandatory IPSec support'.
errata.correction: IPsec support was mandatory only in the early IPv6 node requirements (RFC 4294). RFC 6434 relaxed it from MUST to SHOULD in 2011 and RFC 8504 keeps it there, so IPv6 nodes are recommended, not required, to support IPsec.
